questions.learningObjective: Explain what the stochastic row condition guarantees for a modelled population.
questions.stem: An architect models a building's three zones as states with transition rows summing to one. Explain what this condition guarantees about the modelled population across many rounds.

answer.exemplar: Each row lists the probabilities of leaving one zone for the three zones, so the row totals of one ensure the departing population is fully redistributed. Applied round after round, the total population of the building stays fixed while only its distribution changes.

questions.explanation: Row sums of one are a conservation statement: whatever leaves a zone is accounted for in the destination zones. Repeating the model therefore redistributes a fixed population instead of creating or destroying it.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the Matrix-Tree Theorem counts spanning trees.
questions.stem: An architect must count the ways to connect five structural nodes so that the network is connected and free of cycles. Explain how the Matrix-Tree Theorem provides this count.

answer.exemplar: Build the Laplacian L of the five-node graph, where each diagonal entry is the node's degree and each off-diagonal entry is minus one when two nodes are joined. Deleting any one row and the matching column gives a 4 by 4 minor whose determinant is the number of spanning trees.

questions.explanation: The theorem turns a combinatorial counting question into a determinant, provided the Laplacian is assembled carefully. Any principal minor gives the same answer, so a mistake in one row does not go unnoticed when two choices are compared.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how circulant structure speeds up repeated multiplication.
questions.stem: An architect's layout matrix has rows that are cyclic shifts of one another, so the matrix is circulant. Explain how this structure helps when the matrix must be multiplied many times.

answer.exemplar: A circulant matrix is diagonalised by the discrete Fourier matrix, so its powers can be computed from the eigenvalues instead of by repeated multiplication. Each eigenvalue is the first row evaluated at a root of unity, so one row of data determines the whole spectral picture.

questions.explanation: The cyclic symmetry means the matrix shares eigenvectors with the shift matrix, which makes powering and inverting far cheaper than generic linear algebra. Understanding the structure turns a long iteration into a short spectral calculation.
questions.hint: Cyclic symmetry brings Fourier tools to the problem.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how to find the long-run shares of a two-state chain.
questions.stem: Two zones with transition rows (0.8,0.2) and (0.5,0.5) are modelled by an architect. Explain how to find the long-run share of occupants in each zone.

answer.exemplar: A stationary distribution pi satisfies pi P = pi, so 0.2*pi1 = 0.5*pi2 together with pi1 + pi2 = 1 gives pi1 = 5/7 and pi2 = 2/7. Those shares are the long-run proportions the model predicts for a large building.

questions.explanation: The balance condition says the share leaving a zone equals the share arriving in it, which with two states fixes the ratio. Normalising the two shares to sum to one then gives the full distribution.
questions.hint: Balance the flows into and out of each zone.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why all principal minors of a Laplacian give the same tree count.
questions.stem: An architect needs to count spanning trees for a graph with several nodes and is considering the Matrix-Tree Theorem. Explain how the count relates to a determinant and why choosing different nodes for deletion gives the same answer.

answer.exemplar: The Laplacian has vertex degrees on the diagonal and -1 for each edge elsewhere, and every principal minor has the same determinant, equal to the number of spanning trees. The equality of the minors is a theorem, so verifying two of them is a cheap consistency check on the assembly.

questions.explanation: The Matrix-Tree Theorem guarantees that every principal minor of the Laplacian has the same determinant, which counts the spanning trees. That redundancy is what makes the method reliable despite the fiddly matrix construction.
questions.hint: Every principal minor has the same determinant value.

options.misconception: confuses the row entries with the eigenvalues

options.text: a+d, b+c, a-d, b-c, the row folded into real parts
options.misconception: guesses a real-valued decomposition instead

options.text: The row evaluated at 1, i, -1 and -i, that is a+b+c+d, a+bi-c-di, a-b+c-d and a-bi-c+di
All equal to a+d, since a circulant matrix has one repeated eigenvalue
options.misconception: assumes a single repeated eigenvalue

questions.explanation: The eigenvalues of a circulant matrix are the generating row evaluated at the n-th roots of unity, so for order 4 they come from the points 1, i, -1 and -i. They are generally distinct and often complex even when the matrix is real.
questions.hint: Evaluate the generating row at the roots of unity.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how circulant structure speeds up repeated matrix multiplication.
questions.stem: An architect must multiply a circulant matrix many times when revising a floor plan. Explain how the circulant structure can make this faster than generic matrix multiplication.

answer.exemplar: A circulant matrix is diagonalised by the discrete Fourier matrix, so its powers are obtained by raising its eigenvalues to the desired power and transforming back. Since the eigenvalues come from one row of data evaluated at roots of unity, the work is much less than repeated matrix products.

questions.explanation: Diagonalisation is the payoff of the cyclic symmetry, because the power of a diagonal matrix is found by raising each entry. Generic matrix powering would need many more operations for the same answer.
questions.hint: Think about the Fourier basis for cyclic shifts.

answer.exemplar: The length is the square root of the sum of the squared coordinates, 16 + 4 + 0 + 1 + 9 = 30, so it is the square root of 30, about 5.48. A change in this length means the design has moved a different overall distance from the origin, regardless of direction.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the general procedure for constructing a unit vector.
questions.stem: An architect needs a unit vector pointing along a structural direction in three dimensions. Explain the general procedure and why the result must be checked.
